subject: how could I possibly hierarchically code 'ordered logistic' regression with Matt Trick?

messages.author: 9b1ba46046eac99f
messages.subject: how could I possibly hierarchically code 'ordered logistic' regression with Matt Trick?
parts:
Hi Stan,

I'm currently trying to code a hierarchical ordered logistic regression with Matt Trick, however, I encountered some 'parameter support' problem. 

Say I have the pseudo-code below for a 2-element cutpoint parameter:

parameters {
    ordered[2] thrs_mu;
    vector<lower=0>[2]  thrs_sd;
    ordered[2] thrs_raw[nSubjects];
}

transformed parameters {
    ordered[2] thrs[nSubjects];
    for (s in 1:nSubjects) {
      for (i in 1:2) {
         thrs[s][i]  <- thrs_mu[i] + thrs_sd[i] * thrs_raw[s][i];
    }
  }
}

model {
    thrs_mu  ~ normal(0,1);
    thrs_sd   ~ cauchy(0,5);

    for (s in 1:nSubjects) {
         thrs_raw[s] ~ normal(0,1);
    }

  for (s in 1:nSubjects) {
    for (t in 1:nTrials) {
      bet1[s,t] ~ ordered_logistic( betfun1, thrs[s]) ;
  ...
}

I guess the expression "thrs[s][i]  <- thrs_mu[i] + thrs_sd[i] * thrs_raw[s][i]" could not guarantee that thrs[s][1] is smaller than thrs[s][2]. And I do get a lot error message like "stan::math::ordered_logistic: Cut points parameter is -97.3619, but must be greater than -97.3619", OR like "validate transformed params: thrs[k0__] is not a valid ordered vector. The element at 2 is -5.19271, but should be greater than the previous element, -5.17935".

How could I possibly solve this problem?

One more trick part is that, when I was testing this model with only 1 chain, 10 sample, no warm-up, the model behaved well on my windows laptop, but it threw the above error message on our Linux server. On both machines I use R3.2.0 and Stan2.7.0. 

Any suggestion is welcome. Thanks in advance.
Lei

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] how could I possibly hierarchically code 'ordered logistic' regression with Matt Trick?
parts:
You might get lucky in some cases with inits --- it's probably not
a linux/windows/mac issue. I would think you'd get errors in the transformed
parameter block when the ordering constraint on thrs is violated.

The thing to do is parameterize differences using a log link (i.e., exponentiate
the linear predictor for the difference). That's basically what's going on
in the ordered parameter transform (which isn't used for transformed parameters).


You can also vectorize this:

parts:
Hi Bob, 

thanks for the advice. You are right that error happened during validating the transformed parameter. 
However I wasn't so sure about how to implement the log link? 

I checked the manual (v2.7.0) on page 445 for transforming ordered vector. 
If I understood correctly, do you mean I should implement this transformation 
after the Matt Trick "thrs[s][i]  <- thrs_mu[i] + thrs_sd[i] * thrs_raw[s][i];" 
with an additional unconstrained variable 'y', afterwards, transform 'y' back to 'thrs', and finally in the 
model block define something like 'y ~ normal(0,1)'?

I'd appreciate if you could present a short piece of pseudo code for me to follow.

For vectorizing the 'thrs_raw' parameter, because 'thrs_raw' is a two dimensional vector (i.e. each thrs_raw[s] is a 2-element ordered vector), and I found that Stan does not support real[ , ] ~ normal () yet. So I think I have to do what I had.

Thanks again.
Lei

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] how could I possibly hierarchically code 'ordered logistic' regression with Matt Trick?
parts:
I mean rather than coding the cut points as independent regressions,
code the increment past the previous cut point by exp()-transforming it.

cut[1] <- 0;
for (c in 2:C)
cut[c] <- cut[c-1] + exp(...some predictor...);

Or you can have the first cutpoint be unconstrained. You can use
the non-centered parameterization for the coefficients in the predictor
if you want.

Then you know the sequence cut is increasing. It's a different model
that's been discussed on the list before --- I can't recall what it's
called in the literature. I was surprised that pieces of the literature
try to do what you're doing as it makes the model ill-posed. That is,
the support is restricted to where all the constraints are satisfied,
which itself is data-dependent and can't be easily normalized (not that
we need normalized densities for optimization or MCMC).

- Bob
